ML-systems design: pushback, failure and numbers drills

Three drills for the night before an onsite: thirteen trade-off challenges to defend, failure symptoms to diagnose, and seventeen numbers to know cold. Hide the answers, say yours aloud, then reveal.

Plain wordsCommit, then name what would change your mind

Every pushback has the same good answer shape: the choice, the reason in one number, and the condition under which you would choose differently.

For leadersUsing the drills in a team

The failure drill doubles as an on-call primer for an RL platform team: each row is a symptom, its likely cause and the first check. The numbers drill is the shared vocabulary for capacity reviews.

§18

Pushback drill

When the interviewer challenges a choice, can you defend it with a number and name what would change your mind?

Thirteen challenges you will hear: colocation, strict on-policy training, Ray, FSDP2, storage-based sync, vLLM against SGLang, reusing the serving fleet, plain Docker for sandboxes, the judge as a single point of failure, wrong rewards, verifying sync, what to build first, and cutting cost. Each answer gives the trade-off, a number from this page, and the condition under which you would choose differently.

Answer first, then reveal. A good answer is a choice, a number, and a condition.

  1. “Why not keep it simple and colocate everything?”

    Colocation is the right start: no idle pool, no network sync (CUDA IPC), one placement. It loses when a synchronous step waits on the tail: for the coding run a colocated step takes 33 minutes against 13 for split asynchronous pools. I'd colocate at 64 GPUs and for short single-turn tasks, and split once the slowest trajectory is several times the step's work.

  2. “Why not stay strictly on-policy?”

    Because waiting costs 2.6× here. Two or three versions of staleness with per-token truncated importance weights is stable in practice: Magistral, PipelineRL and AReaL all train asynchronously. Keep a strict synchronous mode for ablations and debugging.

  3. “Why Ray?”

    Actors and placement groups give one driver a programmable view of every engine and trainer rank, and gangs land where I plan them. The cost is a CPU object store, so tensors move over NCCL, NIXL or storage instead. What I need is the single-controller model; Kubernetes jobs with gRPC, or Monarch, would also work. About half the open RL libraries use Ray; prime-rl and PipelineRL run plain processes, and Meta's LlamaRL is plain PyTorch.

  4. “Why FSDP2 and not Megatron?”

    For a 70B dense model FSDP2 is simpler, native to PyTorch and fast enough, and DCP checkpoints reshard on load. For a large MoE I'd take Megatron-Core or TorchTitan for expert and pipeline parallelism. The choice follows the parallelism the model needs and what the team can debug.

  5. “Why not just push weights through S3?”

    Every replica reads the same bytes through shared storage bandwidth, about (1 + R)·S ÷ B. For 76 replicas of a 70B model that is over a minute per step even at 100 GB/s, against 3.5 s over NCCL. Storage is right for versioned recovery and elastic replicas (ModelExpress), not the per-step hot path.

  6. “Why vLLM over SGLang?”

    Either works: both have weight-update, pause and memory-release APIs and both sit under major RL frameworks. I'd pick vLLM for its native weight-transfer backends and model coverage, unless the team already runs SGLang. What matters is token-in/token-out, log-probs, routed experts and a tested sync path.

  7. “Can't we use the production serving fleet for rollouts?”

    Share the engine, the images and the operations, not the fleet. RL changes weights every step, needs pause and log-probs, and would wreck serving latency targets; borrowing idle serving GPUs off-peak for separate RL replicas is fine. The exception is LoRA RL, where one multi-LoRA pool can serve many adapters.

  8. “Plain Docker for model-written code? Shouldn't that be gVisor?”

    It is Docker images either way; the runtime is one line. On a dedicated, egress-blocked sandbox cluster with no credentials inside, plain runc is what most open RL-for-code stacks run, and it is where I'd start. I'd switch to gVisor or a microVM when sandboxes share nodes with other teams' work, need network or root, or run other tenants' code, or when the policy is strong enough that an escape becomes a plausible reward hack. Either way, I'd measure gVisor's cost on the build-heavy tasks before choosing.

  9. “Your judge is a single point of failure.”

    It is a stateless pool behind a queue: replicas fail independently, the queue applies backpressure, requests are idempotent and cached, and a failed judgement voids the sample rather than scoring zero, so the trainer never learns from an outage.

  10. “What if the reward is wrong?”

    Treat reward functions as code: unit tests, a golden set of trajectories with known scores, versions, and a daily audit of the highest-reward samples, where hacking shows up first. Alert when training reward rises while held-out evaluation falls.

  11. “How do you know a weight sync worked?”

    Three checks: per-shard checksums on a sample every sync and on all shards daily; canary prompts whose engine log-probs must match the trainer's within a k3 KL threshold; and the version carried by every sample, so a lagging replica shows up in the staleness histogram.

  12. “You have four engineers and a quarter. What do you build first?”

    Adopt before building: an open framework (verl, SkyRL, prime-rl or NeMo-RL), or vLLM, FSDP2 and Ray directly. Build the sandbox service and the telemetry, because those are specific to our tasks, and defer multi-tenancy and custom sync until the numbers say we need them.

  13. “Cut the cost by 30%.”

    Measure the waste first: groups dropped for equal rewards, void samples, stale drops, re-prefills after cache eviction. Then FP8 rollouts and cache, a CPU cache tier, tighter packing in the trainer, preemptible capacity for rollout replicas, and a smaller or cached judge.

§19

Failure drill

Given a symptom from a running RL job, can you name the likely cause, the first thing you would check, and the fix?

Twelve symptoms, from reward hacking and engine upgrades that shift the k3 KL, through starved trainers, cache evictions, hangs and bad syncs, to flaky tests, length blow-ups, out-of-memory steps and a single garbage replica. The pattern is always the same: look at the trace or metric that separates the hypotheses before touching anything.

For each symptom: cause, first check, fix.

  1. Training reward climbs; held-out evaluation falls.

    Cause: reward hacking, or a shift between training and evaluation tasks. Check: read the highest-reward samples. Fix: close the loophole (hidden tests, read-only paths, a judge check), then re-evaluate.

  2. Engine-versus-trainer k3 KL jumps after an engine upgrade.

    Cause: a kernel or precision change (attention backend, FP8 path, sampler). Check: canary prompts on old and new engines at fixed weights. Fix: pin the version, use an FP32 LM head, keep truncated IS on, and gate upgrades on the canary.

  3. Step time doubles and trainer GPUs sit idle.

    Cause: the buffer runs dry: a long tail, slow sandboxes or a judge backlog. Check: buffer depth and the generate, tool and score latency histograms. Fix: more trajectories in flight, timeouts, more sandboxes or judge replicas.

  4. Rollout throughput sags over several hours.

    Cause: prefix-cache evictions forcing re-prefill, or preemptions under cache pressure. Check: vLLM's prefix-cache hit rate and preemption counters per replica. Fix: session affinity, a CPU cache tier, fewer live trajectories per replica.

  5. The trainer hangs with no error.

    Cause: a rank died or entered a different collective. Check: NCCL flight-recorder dumps and the last step each rank reached. Fix: kill, exclude the bad node, restart from the checkpoint, tighten the watchdog.

  6. Rewards collapse right after a weight sync.

    Cause: a wrong parameter mapping on the engines: a missed fused tensor, a quantization scale, tied embeddings. Check: /weight_checker checksums and canary log-probs against the trainer. Fix: correct the mapping and make the canary a gate before resume.

  7. Clip fraction and importance weights spike.

    Cause: staleness beyond the cap, or a replica stuck on an old version. Check: the staleness histogram and per-replica versions. Fix: lower the cap, drain lagging replicas, inspect the sync.

  8. The sandbox error rate reaches 10%.

    Cause: image-pull throttling, full node disks, or a bad base image. Check: errors by node and by image, and registry limits. Fix: prefetch and cache images, garbage-collect, roll back the image.

  9. The same patch gets different rewards on reruns.

    Cause: flaky tests or a nondeterministic judge. Check: grade the same patch five times. Fix: quarantine flaky tasks; temperature 0 and a pinned judge version.

  10. Response length explodes.

    Cause: the reward favours length, truncation counts as success, or a masking bug. Check: reward against length, and the masks of truncated samples. Fix: length-aware normalization, correct masks, token caps.

  11. The trainer runs out of memory on some steps only.

    Cause: an outlier sequence length in a micro-batch. Check: tokens per micro-batch at the failing step. Fix: token-budget packing, length caps, context parallelism for the longest sequences.

  12. One replica returns garbage; the others are fine.

    Cause: a partial or failed sync on that replica. Check: its version and checksums. Fix: drain it, re-sync from the published version, and make each replica's commit atomic.

§20

Rapid-fire numbers

Which numbers should you be able to say without a calculator?

Seventeen: H100 compute, memory and links; KV bytes per token; vLLM's cache block and step budget; trainer FLOPs per token; decode and prefill speed; weight bytes and broadcast times at 70B and 1T; checkpoint bytes per parameter; the interruption rate and the Young–Daly interval; Little's law; task-image sizes; the trainer's share of an agentic step; TTFT and TPOT; vLLM's pause modes; and what dominates a long-context decode step.

Say the number, then the one-line reason.

  1. H100: compute, memory, links?

    989 TFLOP/s BF16 dense (1,979 FP8), 80 GB at 3.35 TB/s, NVLink 450 GB/s each way, 400 Gb/s ≈ 50 GB/s of network per GPU.

  2. KV bytes per token for a Llama-70B shape?

    2 × 80 layers × 8 KV heads × 128 × 2 bytes = 320 KiB in BF16, 160 KiB in FP8: 5.2 GB for a 32K-token trajectory.

  3. vLLM's cache block and step budget?

    16 tokens per block; 8,192 tokens per step by default for the server on an H100 (16,384 offline), and up to 1,024 sequences at once. Preemption frees the newest request's blocks when they run out.

  4. Trainer FLOPs per token for 70B?

    6N ≈ 424 GFLOP; 8N ≈ 565 with log-prob recompute; attention adds about 30% more at 32K tokens.

  5. Decode tokens/s per H100: 70B, FP8 cache, 17K context?

    At most η·BW ÷ (kv × context) ≈ 700; about 500 with 4-GPU replicas. Each sequence moves at about 26 tokens/s.

  6. Prefill cost per token for 70B in FP8?

    2N = 141 GFLOP at about 790 TFLOP/s (40% of FP8 peak): 0.18 ms of H100 time. Prefill is compute-bound, decode memory-bound.

  7. 70B weights, and their broadcast time?

    70 GB in FP8, 141 GB in BF16: 1.8 s and 3.5 s at 40 GB/s.

  8. A 1T model's weight sync?

    BF16 broadcast about 52 s at 40 GB/s (Miles' NCCL broadcast of Kimi-K2, about 1 TB in FP8, took 53 s); sharded FP8 point-to-point 1–7 s in practice; Perplexity 1.3 s.

  9. Checkpoint bytes per parameter with Adam?

    12: FP32 master weights plus two moments. In memory with gradients, 16 bytes of sharded state.

  10. How often does a GPU job get interrupted?

    About once per 2,100 GPU-days (Llama 3): every 2 days at 1,024 GPUs, every 12 hours at 4,096, every 3 hours at 16,384.

  11. How often should you checkpoint?

    Young–Daly: √(2 × blocking time × MTBF). 1 s blocking and a 70-hour MTBF give about 12 minutes.

  12. How many sandboxes for the coding run?

    Little's law: rate × lifetime = 10.6/s × 674 s ≈ 7,100, about 14,000 vCPUs.

  13. How big is a SWE task environment?

    1–2.5 GB per task image; preparing one took about 90 s with Docker. Fork from a snapshot instead of preparing G times.

  14. What share of a coding-agent step's GPU-hours is training?

    About 70% at 32K tokens per trajectory: the trainer processes 2.6× more tokens than decode makes, three to four passes each. That holds only while later turns hit the prefix cache; re-prefilling every turn would make rollouts the bigger pool.

  15. TTFT, TPOT, goodput?

    Time to first token (queueing plus prefill), time per output token after it (one decode step), and goodput: requests per second that meet both targets.

  16. vLLM's pause modes?

    abort drops in-flight requests, wait lets them finish, keep freezes them and resumes them after the update.

  17. What dominates a long-context decode step?

    Reading every sequence's KV cache, not the weights, so larger batches stop helping once cache reads dominate.
